newsitem.title: UK: UK output data suggest early rate rise off agenda.
newsitem.headline: UK output data suggest early rate rise off agenda.

text.p: A surprise fall in UK manufacturing output in August suggests the industrial recovery is still fragile and makes a pre-election rate rise look even more improbable, analysts said on Monday.

"The figures are a timely reminder that the manufacturing sector is not out of the woods yet despite the upswing in domestic demand," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS."They confirm that an early rate rise is clearly off the agenda."
Manufacturing output fell 0.3 percent in August for a year-on-year fall of 0.9 percent.
The figures were in stark contract to the more sanguine assessment of the manufacturing sector contained in the latest CIPS' purchasing managers and CBI surveys.
The purchasing managers survey reported that in September, firms recorded the largest monthly increases in output and new orders since the autumn of 1994.
The official figures lag survey evidence and many analysts expect September data will show something of a bounce back.
But a new threat overhangs the troubled manufacturing sector. If sterling continues to appreciate, it could damage the tentative recovery seen in demand for British goods abroad.

"Export markets are crucial for the manufacturing sector and a further loss of competitiveness for UK firms -- due to a further appreciation of the pound -- could stifle any manufacturing recovery before it really begins," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
UK manufacturers are at the mercy of overseas demand since consumer durables account for just six percent of total production.
Sterling has appreciated by almost 4.0 percent in the last two months on a trade-weighted basis, although the rally from the last rate cut on June 6 is a more modest 1.5 percent.

The figures suggest excess stocks are still keeping output in check. Manufacturers have made inroads into the overhang and second quarter GDP data showed firms ran down inventories to the tune of 250 million stg.
But this made only a tiny dent in the ratio of stocks to ouput which is still around the 90 percent level.

"Firms have been able to meet the new demand by selling goods off the shelves rather than stepping up production. It looks like this will continue to dampen output for a little longer, but it should only be a temporary drag," said Loynes.

But the frail recovery in the sector will give Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke some ammunition to help resist calls for a rate rise that are sure to come from Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George in the months ahead.
"With manufacturing still in the doldrums, there is no chance Clarke will give in to George's requests for a rise in (5.75 percent) base rates," said Loynes.
Financial markets appear to agree. The short sterling strip suggests the first half-point rate rise will not take place until June 1997, after the next general election.
